title: Dearly Beloved, We Are Gathered Here Today to Get Through This Thing Called... Implementation.
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes uses two decades of school-leadership observation, dressed up as "Fifty Shades of Implementation," to argue that school quality assurance is broken because it measures compliance rather than understanding. Her twelve named implementation failure modes -- the "photocopier model" where a crisp idea degrades through six meetings and three PowerPoints, the "learning-walk miracle" where a technique's use spikes only while leaders are visibly watching, and the "mental-model problem" where staff share vocabulary but not meaning -- describe how a whole-school priority routinely collapses into a single misapplied technique (mini-whiteboards) by the time it reaches classrooms. Her constructive argument is that QA should diagnose mental models, not just observable performance: two teachers can run an identical-looking routine from entirely different understandings of its purpose, and only the deeper interrogation reveals which one will produce intelligent adaptation versus "technique theatre." She reframes implementation as a chain (intended model, interpreted model, enacted practice, pupil experience) with middle leaders as the critical, under-trained translation point, and proposes replacing the standard train-then-QA sequence with a cycle that folds diagnosis and re-adaptation back into ongoing quality assurance.
points: Hughes's central claim is that school QA typically measures whether staff perform a visible technique rather than what they understand the technique is for, which is why compliance can spike during a learning walk and vanish once leaders leave the room.

Her "photocopier model" names how a clear senior-leadership idea degrades in fidelity as it passes through layers of meetings and briefings, until a whole-school priority like "checking for understanding" collapses into a single narrow technique like mini-whiteboards.

She distinguishes two teachers who can look identical on a learning walk while operating from opposite mental models -- one performing a technique for observation, the other using it to gather information to adapt instruction -- and argues only the second produces real intelligent adaptation.

Her proposed fix replaces the standard "train then QA" sequence with a cycle -- define, train, enact, QA, diagnose, develop or adapt, enact again -- that treats QA as an ongoing diagnostic tool for surfacing which of several possible failure points (knowledge, skill, belief, environment, or the implementation design itself) is actually blocking a practice.
quotes: The photocopier model of implementation: Senior leadership puts a beautifully crisp idea into the machine. By the time it has passed through six meetings, three PowerPoints and a departmental briefing, everyone is holding a slightly grey version with one corner missing.
Remarkably, use of mini-whiteboards increased by 600% during the 40 minutes in which senior leaders were walking around carrying clipboards.
We thought we had achieved alignment because everyone was using the same vocabulary. Unfortunately, they were using the same words to describe six different things.

One may think, "I need to demonstrate this technique during an observation." Another may think, "I need information about what pupils understand so I can decide what to do next." The second mental model is much more likely to produce intelligent adaptation than the first, which just becomes technique theatre.
The real test of whether something is embedded isn't whether people do it during a learning walk. It's whether they still do it in February, period 5, when the Wi-Fi has gone down.

Policies and checklists can create surface compliance, but they cannot specify the correct response to every situation. Instead, the more scalable approach is to develop shared, accurate mental models among the people making those decisions.
